# Theme 3 Review

<!-- This file is the source of a page on the course website. Read it there: https://ai.buas.nl/open-courses/introduction-to-ml/self-study/theme-3/05_review.html -->

You have learned to evaluate and compare models, and you have looked inside three of them. This page sums up the theme and checks the main ideas.

## Summary

- [Modeling & Evaluation](01_modeling_and_evaluation.ipynb): cross-validation for a reliable estimate (stratified for classification, by group when samples belong together); a validation set or cross-validation for every choice, and the test set once at the end; feature selection, model selection and hyperparameter tuning; underfitting and overfitting from the training and validation errors; metrics such as precision, recall, (macro-)F1, MAE, RMSE and R².
- [Linear Regression](02_linear_regression.ipynb): a cost, gradient descent, several features, polynomial features, and regularization with Ridge and Lasso.
- [Logistic Regression](03_logistic_regression.ipynb): from a line to a probability, the decision threshold, precision-recall and ROC curves, and regularization with `C`.
- [Clustering](04_clustering.ipynb): distances and scaling, K-Means, the elbow method and the silhouette score, and density-based clustering.

## Quiz

These questions are easy if you have worked through the activities. Choose an answer to see whether it is right and why.

::: {.quiz data-answer="2"}
A model has a training error close to 0 and a much higher validation error. What is the most likely diagnosis?

- Underfitting: the model is too simple for the data. [Underfitting shows as a high training error. Here the training error is close to 0.]{.feedback}
- Overfitting: the model follows the noise in its training data. [Right. A large gap between training and validation error is the sign.]{.feedback}
- A bug in the metric, because the training and the validation error should be about equal. [The two errors are rarely equal: the training error is usually lower.]{.feedback}
:::

::: {.quiz data-answer="3"}
You compare ten values of a hyperparameter. On which data do you compare them?

- On the test set, because it gives the most honest estimate of the performance on new data. [Once you choose on the test set, its score is no longer honest.]{.feedback}
- On the training data, because the model was fitted on it. [The training error keeps going down for more flexible settings, so it would always pick the most flexible one.]{.feedback}
- On a validation set, or with cross-validation. [Right. The test set stays unseen until the final check.]{.feedback}
:::

::: {.quiz data-answer="2"}
95% of the samples are negative, and a model predicts "negative" for every sample. Which metric shows the problem?

- Accuracy, which is 95%, because it counts every correct prediction. [95% looks good, and that is the problem: accuracy hides it.]{.feedback}
- The F1 score of the positive class, or the macro-F1. [Right. The F1 of the positive class is 0, so the macro-F1 is low too.]{.feedback}
- The mean absolute error of the predictions, computed on the test set. [The MAE is a regression metric.]{.feedback}
:::

::: {.quiz data-answer="1"}
In `LogisticRegression`, what does a larger value of `C` do?

- It weakens the regularization. [Right. `C` works in the inverse direction of the regularization strength.]{.feedback}
- It strengthens the regularization, so the model becomes simpler and smoother. [The other way around: a smaller `C` means stronger regularization.]{.feedback}
- It moves the decision threshold away from 0.5. [The threshold is a separate choice, made after training.]{.feedback}
:::

::: {.quiz data-answer="2"}
Why do you scale the features before K-Means?

- Because K-Means only accepts values between 0 and 1, like a probability. [K-Means accepts any numbers. The problem is what the distances mean.]{.feedback}
- Because K-Means uses distances, which large numbers dominate. [Right. Scaling gives every feature a comparable influence.]{.feedback}
- Because scaling sets the number of clusters that K-Means looks for. [You choose the number of clusters yourself, for example with the elbow method or the silhouette score.]{.feedback}
:::
